sentences.text: On 23 September 2026, the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival, a coalition of various Ethiopian rebel and insurgent groups, launched a large-scale military offensive against the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) described the offensive as a defensive war against the federal government of Ethiopia.
The TPLF took control of several towns bordering Tigray Region.
Control shifted back to federal forces, with the ENDF retaking control of Afar towns and capturing the Tigray capital Mekelle.
Eritrean troops entered Tigray while the ENDF continued advancing north in Tigray Region.
The offensive is the largest escalation in fighting since the Tigray war (2020–2022), which was one of the bloodiest conflicts of the 21st century.
The TPLF was effectively the ruling party of Ethiopia, dominating the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) from 1991 to 2018.
In 2018, Abiy Ahmed was elected leader of the EPRDF and thus became prime minister.
The Tigray war took place under Abiy's leadership from November 2020 to November 2022, when Ethiopia and the TPLF signed the Pretoria agreement.

The situation remained unstable, with officials from the Amhara Region continuing to occupy Western Tigray and the government launching a series of drone strikes in 2025 while the TPLF amassed troops at the border.

In May 2025, the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) revoked the TPLF's registration as a political party, despite the TPLF being a signatory, alongside the federal government, to the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray War.

In response, the TPLF declared the restoration of the pre-war administration and installed the TPLF's chairman Debretsion Gebremichael as Tigray's regional president, creating a rival government to that of the pro-government Interim Regional Administration of Tigray.

In late January and early February 2026, days-long clashes erupted in Tigray between the TPLF and the ENDF, in what Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) described as the most significant fighting between the two since full-scale war.
Relations between the central government and TPLF continued to deteriorate, and by mid-July the TPLF declared the Pretoria agreement "effectively dead".
On 1 August, a battle lasting several hours broke out between the ENDF and the TPLF near the Sudan border.
In subsequent weeks, the ENDF carried out numerous drone strikes in Tigray.

The regional capital of Mekelle was hit by a series of drone strikes in late August, including an attack on 20 August against a residential compound with no obvious military targets that wounded 13 civilians.

sentences.section: 29 September–11 October 2026: Addis Ababa strikes, Eritrean troops and continued hostilities
sentences.text: On 14 October, Fano claimed to have captured the town of Meragna in Amhara's North Shewa Zone.
ENDF troops took control of Zalambessa on 12 October.
EPFAS troops had left earlier.
EPFAS troops took control of Fatsi, Adi Daero, Adi Nbried, Adi Hageray, and Adi Awala.
The UN Security Council (UNSC) held a closed-door meeting on the situation in the Horn of Africa.
The Security Council Report (SCR) argued that UNSC members seemed "increasingly concerned about the interstate dimension of the recent escalation".
On 16 October, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed announced the formation of a new interim government for the Tigray Region intended to operate for six months before holding elections.
Four chief executives were appointed, with the President of the Executive Committee position expected to rotate between the four.
Most of the officials appointed to the interim government had previously split from the TPLF.
The takeover of the three Tigray Region airports by Tigrayan forces was a violation of the Pretoria Agreement according to the African Union (AU) Commission (AUC) chairperson, Mahamoud Ali Youssouf.
On 23 September 2026, Youssouf requested Olusegun Obasanjo, African Union High Representative for the Horn of Africa, to carry out negotiations to preserve the peace process.
On 2 October, Amnesty International called for the AU Peace and Security Council to hold an emergency session, arguing that the AU "was one of the guarantors" of the Pretoria Agreement.
Bloomberg reported that Ethiopia plans to withdraw 3,000 soldiers from Somalia.
Somalia said it had been not informed of such plans.
It was not immediately known whether or how a withdrawal would impact the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia or other, bilateral deployments.

On 1 October 2026, the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced it was shutting its embassy in Asmara due to the alleged Eritrean involvement in the conflict and expelled 10 diplomats ordering them to leave the country within 48 hours and declaring them as persona non grata.
In response, Eritrea announced the severance of all diplomatic ties with its Ministry of Foreign Affairs saying on X that it, "had no choice but to reciprocate".

Eritrea stated that one of its fears was that Ethiopia would utilize the conflict to initiate an offensive on the port of Assab, and added that Ethiopia's latest escalations signified a "publicly pronounced declaration of war" and an attempt at regime change.

On 5 October, Abiy was sworn in for another term as Prime Minister of Ethiopia, and in a speech immediately after he stated that he would "work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea".

Beginning with the onset of the Tigray war in November 2020, acute food shortages leading to death and starvation became widespread in northern Ethiopia, and the Tigray, Afar and Amhara Regions in particular.
While the situation improved after the March 2022 truce and allowed for humanitarian distribution of food, the lack of rain in the spring of 2022 compounded the already existing food insecurity.
The resurgence of fighting after the ceasefire collapsed in August 2022 exacerbated the situation even more; by October, between 400 and 900 a day were dying of starvation.

As of October 2026, areas in the southern Tigray were facing droughts which prolonged food insecurity into "crisis-level conditions" as classified by Phase 3 of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
Fighting disrupted fuel supplies, market activity, transportation, harvests—physically and monetarily restricting access to food, farmland, labor opportunities, and other essential goods.
According to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET), these conditions risked the IPC Phase 3 conditions continuing.

Due to the intense fighting in Northern Ethiopia, the internet connection in the area was disrupted, alongside telephone lines, which prevented news agencies and families from contacting external regions and individuals within the region itself.

According to Human Rights Watch (HRW), the ENDF 20 August strike against the Daero area of Mekelle, during the leadup to the September conflict, was "unlawfully indiscriminate" since it had "no evident military targets".
HRW's evidence included interviews with three survivors, two medical workers, and two residents, and analysis of photographic, video, and satellite evidence.
The 20 August attack was the dropping of a bomb by an aircraft on a residential compound for teachers around 11:00 local time.
A diameter crater resulted from the bombing.
HRW recommended investigation into the 20 August Daero attack as a possible war crime.
Witnesses speaking to The Guardian reported a campaign of forced recruitment by rebels in Tigray, including the conscription at gunpoint of children as young as 15.
: The Department of Foreign Affairs advised its citizens against unnecessary travel to Ethiopia, and issued a Do Not Travel warning to the conflict areas.
: According to Washington Examiner, the United States (US) advised its citizens against traveling to the Tigray and Afar regions and prohibited U.S. government personnel from traveling there.
The United States Department of State released a statement urging both Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint, citing cross-border "tensions".
: UN Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk urged all parties to immediately de-escalate tensions and prevent a return to full scale war.
Vatican City: Pope Leo XIV extended a plea to "all parties to choose the path of dialogue" and expressed hope for international humanitarian aid.

Critical Threats concluded that the EPFAS "offensive likely aims to consolidate the [TDF/TPLF]’s control of Tigray and its rear supply lines, relieve federal pressure on the region, and pressure key federal supply lines."

Despite concluding that EPFAS would indeed concern the government and would likely not agree to de-escalation measures, experts from the International Crisis Group (ICG) questioned the group's collaborative capabilities.

The Dynamics International Group corroborated that the "show of force and unity and military preparedness to wage asymmetrical warfare," underscored by being "unlikely to match the military power of the ENDF," would make their insurgency likely to only reach through the "short to mid-term period."
Dynamics International said short-term intensification could occur thanks to foreign involvement from Egypt, Sudan, and Eritrea.

Following the Sudanese government's accusation of Ethiopian involvement in March 2026, Alan Boswell of the International Crisis Group (ICG), predicting the beginning of the Ethiopian offensive, said that it "could merge with the conflict raging in Sudan, creating an unpredictable regional conflagration."
Experts from The Soufan Center (TSC) added that the "porous borders" of countries within the Horn.
Boswell underscored that Saudi Arabia and the UAE's backing of belligerents in the Horn of Africa "ma[de] the situation even more combustible."

Modern Diplomacy argued on 4 October that the fighting in Ethiopia and that in Yemen should be considered a single conflict, given overlapping interests of Red Sea actors like Egypt; it said conflicts "merge when they share terrain, patrons and consequences".
It forecast a 25% chance of war reaching the coast with an Ethiopian advance towards Assab, and 75% chance of either a contained, intrastate conflict in Ethiopia or a broad, negotiated settlement.
It argued the latter would require mediation by the AU and Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, and a long-term port deal for Ethiopia through Assab, Berbera or Djibouti.

Abdurahman Sayed, Director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration, stated that Ethiopia wanted Eritrea to get involved in order to seize the opportunity to occupy the strategic port of Assab; He further stated that the Eritrean troops did not necessarily need to actually be in Ethiopian territory to fabricate a casus belli.

The Albanian news service Nacionale stated that unnamed analysts warned about Eritrea possibly being dragged into the war, also noting the expanding ongoing Ethiopian mobilization on the Eritrean border.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Ethiopia westerly borders Sudan, which has been entrenched in a civil war since 2023.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Two primary belligerents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), fight along an East–West divide.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Ethiopia involved itself in the present conflict in February 2026, when researchers from Reuters conducted a visual investigation revealing Ethiopia's hosting of a training camp for RSF militants, set along the two countries' border, specifically the Blue Nile State, where the RSF since launched a new front.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Compounded by accusations of Ethiopian-launched drone strikes into Sudan, the Sudanese government subsequently accused Ethiopia of its involvement in the civil war a month later, in March.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Ethiopia's support for the RSF facilitated the RSF's efforts in the southeastern front it launched in January, along Sudan's border with Ethiopia, including allowing the RSF to launch offensives from Ethiopian territory as reported in August.

sentences.section: Ethiopian involvement in the Sudanese Civil War
sentences.text: Foreign involvement has been a cornerstone of the civil war's intractability, with primary funding of the SAF coming from Saudi Arabia and the RSF from the United Arab Emirates (UAE)—funding which has been labelled as containing elements of proxy conflict, extractivism, and a Saudi Arabian-Emirati rivalry.

sentences.section: Somali Civil War spillover into Ethiopia
sentences.text: Ethiopia easterly borders Somalia, which has also entrenched in a civil war since between 1978 and 1991, with the present phase beginning in 2009.

sentences.section: Somali Civil War spillover into Ethiopia
sentences.text: It is being fought between the internationally-recognized Somali government's military wing, the Somali National Army (SNA); the Somali Future Council, an opposition coalition; Islamic State (IS)-affiliated groups including al-Shabaab and Somalia Wilayah; and the self-declared state of Somaliland.

sentences.section: Somali Civil War spillover into Ethiopia
sentences.text: On the military front, Al-Shabaab regained much of its territorial losses in the 2022–2023 government offensive thanks it part to deepening ties with the Houthis in Yemen—another ongoing conflict being waged across the Bab al-Mandab Strait from the Horn and more recently within it, since September 2026—risking escalation in the Somali civil war, as further complicated by warnings of the African Union (AU) Support and Stabilization Mission's (AUSSOM) potential collapse following the cessation of US funding beyond December of that year.

sentences.section: Somali Civil War spillover into Ethiopia
sentences.text: On the diplomatic front, Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in January 2024, giving Ethiopia access to the Red Sea through the Port of Berbera in return for its recognition of Somaliland.

sentences.section: Somali Civil War spillover into Ethiopia
sentences.text: Despite agreeing to restore bilateral relations through the Ankara Declaration—signed in Turkey that following December—through which it restating its recognition of Somalia's sovereign territory, analysts underscored that it created a precarious peace.
